stem: Which item is shown in the **trading section** of the income statement (statement of profit or loss)?

options.rationale: Correct: the cost of bringing purchases in is part of cost of sales.
Delivering goods to customers is a selling expense below gross profit.
Discount allowed is an expense in the profit and loss section.
Rent received is other income, added after gross profit.

explanation: The trading section holds revenue, sales returns and the cost of sales items: inventories, purchases, purchases returns and carriage inwards.

stem: The inventory figure shown in a trial balance prepared at the year end is the …

options.content: inventory at the start of the year
options.rationale: Correct: the closing count is made after the ledger is balanced and is given as a note.

options.content: inventory at the end of the year
options.rationale: Closing inventory is not yet in the ledger when the trial balance is drawn up.

options.content: average inventory held during the year
options.rationale: Average inventory is used in ratio analysis, not in the trial balance.
Goods bought during the year are purchases.

explanation: Inventory in the trial balance is opening inventory; closing inventory is a note below it.

stem: Nyasha's revenue was US\$64,200 and sales returns were US\$900. Opening inventory was US\$5,300, purchases US\$41,800 and closing inventory US\$6,100. What was her gross profit?

options.rationale: This forgets to deduct the sales returns from revenue.
This adds closing inventory instead of deducting it.
This uses purchases as cost of sales and ignores both inventories.

stem: How is **discount received** treated in the income statement?

options.content: Deducted from purchases in cost of sales
options.rationale: Cash discount is a finance gain, not a reduction in the cost of goods; trade discount is never recorded.

options.content: Deducted from gross profit as an expense
options.rationale: That is the treatment of discount allowed.

options.content: Added to gross profit as other income
options.rationale: Correct: it is a gain from paying suppliers promptly.

options.content: Deducted from revenue with the sales returns
options.rationale: Only sales returns are deducted from revenue.

explanation: Discount received is other income; discount allowed is an expense.

stem: Which item does **not** appear in the income statement of a sole trader?

options.rationale: Depreciation is an expense of the year.
They are deducted from purchases in cost of sales.

options.content: Drawings of cash by the owner
options.rationale: Correct: drawings reduce capital in the statement of financial position.
Commission received is other income.

explanation: Drawings are a withdrawal of capital by the owner, not an expense of earning income.

stem: Opening inventory US\$4,600; purchases US\$38,900; carriage inwards US\$720; purchases returns US\$640; closing inventory US\$5,250. What is the cost of sales?

options.rationale: Carriage inwards has been deducted instead of added.
Purchases returns have been added instead of deducted.
Closing inventory has not been deducted: this is the cost of goods available for sale.

hints: Returns reduce purchases; carriage inwards increases them.

stem: Closing inventory was **overstated** by US\$500. What is the effect on the income statement?

options.content: Cost of sales is overstated, so gross profit is understated by US\$500
options.rationale: This is the effect of understating closing inventory.

options.content: Cost of sales is understated, so gross profit is overstated by US\$500
options.rationale: Correct: a larger deduction makes cost of sales too small.

options.content: Revenue is overstated by US\$500, so gross profit rises
options.rationale: Inventory does not affect revenue.

options.content: Gross profit is correct, but expenses are overstated by US\$500
options.rationale: Inventory is in the trading section, not among the expenses.

explanation: Closing inventory is subtracted to find cost of sales; subtracting too much makes cost of sales too low and gross profit (and profit for the year) too high.
hints: Closing inventory is deducted in cost of sales.

stem: Which business would prepare an income statement **without** a trading section?

options.content: A tuck shop at a school in Gweru
options.rationale: A tuck shop buys and resells goods.
Correct: it sells a service, so it has no cost of goods sold.

options.content: A wholesaler of maize meal in Harare
options.rationale: A wholesaler buys and resells goods.
A hardware shop buys and resells goods.

explanation: Service businesses earn fees; they have no purchases of goods for resale and so no gross profit.

stem: Gross profit was US\$27,400, discount received US\$1,350 and total expenses US\$18,900. What was the profit for the year (net profit)?

options.rationale: Discount received has been treated as an expense.
Discount received has been left out.
Expenses have been added instead of deducted.

explanation: Profit for the year = gross profit + other income − expenses = 27,400 + 1,350 − 18,900 = 9,850.

stem: Carriage outwards is added to purchases in the cost of sales calculation.
explanation: False. Carriage outwards is the cost of delivering goods to customers: a selling expense. Only carriage inwards is added to purchases.

stem: The heading of an income statement should read "for the year ended 31 December 2025", not "at 31 December 2025".
explanation: True. The income statement covers a period; "at" is used for the statement of financial position, which shows one date.

stem: Match each item with its treatment in the income statement.
explanation: Returns inwards reduce revenue; carriage inwards and returns outwards adjust purchases; discount received is other income; carriage outwards is an expense.

stem: Complete the formulas.

payload.template: Cost of sales = opening inventory + purchases + carriage inwards − purchases returns − {{blank:a}}. Gross profit = revenue − sales returns − {{blank:b}}. Profit for the year = gross profit + {{blank:c}} − expenses.

explanation: These three lines are the skeleton of every trading business's income statement.

stem: Revenue US\$52,700; sales returns US\$1,150; cost of sales US\$33,480. Calculate the gross profit.
explanation: 52,700 − 1,150 − 33,480 = 18,070. Forgetting the sales returns gives 19,220.

stem: Farai's transport business had gross profit of US\$15,600. Other income: rent received US\$2,400, commission received US\$380. Expenses: wages US\$6,200, insurance US\$3,600, fuel US\$1,450, licences US\$980, telephone US\$720, repairs US\$2,650. Calculate the profit for the year (net profit).
explanation: Total other income 2,780; total expenses 15,600. Profit = 15,600 + 2,780 − 15,600 = 2,780. Treating the income as expenses gives (2,780) (a loss).
workedSolution: 1. Total other income 2,780; total expenses 15,600. Profit = 15,600 + 2,780 − 15,600 = 2,780. Treating the income as expenses gives (2,780) (a loss).
hints: Add the other income to gross profit before deducting the total expenses.

stem: Rudo's cost of sales for 2025 was US\$45,950. Her opening inventory was US\$6,800 and purchases were US\$47,300. Calculate her closing inventory.
explanation: Closing inventory = 6,800 + 47,300 − 45,950 = 8,150. Getting the signs of the inventories the wrong way round gives 5,450.
workedSolution: 1. Closing inventory = 6,800 + 47,300 − 45,950 = 8,150. Getting the signs of the inventories the wrong way round gives 5,450.
hints: Cost of sales = opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory. Rearrange.

stem: A driving school earned fees of US\$28,700 and had expenses of US\$31,250. Calculate the loss for the year (enter the amount without a minus sign).
explanation: 31,250 − 28,700 = 2,550 loss: expenses were greater than income.
workedSolution: 1. 31,250 − 28,700 = 2,550 loss: expenses were greater than income.

stem: Explain why closing inventory is deducted when calculating cost of sales.

points.description: Closing inventory is goods bought (or held) but not yet sold
Cost of sales must include only the cost of goods actually sold in the year (matching)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The goods still in the shop at the year end have not been sold, so their cost belongs to next year. Deducting them leaves only the cost of the goods sold, which is matched with this year's revenue.

explanation: Matching: the cost of unsold goods is carried forward to the next period.

stem: Thandeka's gross profit rose this year but her profit for the year fell. Suggest **three** possible reasons.

points.description: Expenses rose (e.g. higher wages, rent or electricity)
Other income fell (e.g. less rent or commission received)
A new or larger non-cash expense, e.g. more depreciation / irrecoverable debts

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Her running expenses such as wages or rent may have risen faster than gross profit; she may have earned less other income such as rent received; and she may have had larger charges such as depreciation on new equipment or irrecoverable debts.

explanation: Anything below gross profit can explain the difference.
hints: Profit for the year = gross profit + other income − expenses.
